bib.title: FEVER: a large-scale dataset for Fact Extraction and VERification

question: Can a large-scale dataset of claims verified against Wikipedia, with sentence-level evidence, be built and how hard is it for a retrieval plus entailment pipeline?
contributions: FEVER dataset of 185,445 claims labelled SUPPORTED, REFUTED or NOTENOUGHINFO with sentence-level evidence
Pipeline baseline (document retrieval, sentence selection, RTE) with oracle analyses

method.summary: Annotators extract and mutate claims from Wikipedia intro sentences (June 2017 dump), then a separate group labels each claim and records evidence sentences. A three-stage baseline (DrQA TF-IDF document retrieval, TF-IDF sentence selection, entailment classifier) is evaluated with oracle ablations.
method.task: claim verification against Wikipedia (retrieval of evidence plus 3-way classification)

datasets.name: FEVER
datasets.size: 185,445 claims; Table 1: train 80,035+29,775+35,639, dev 3,333 per class, test 3,333 per class, reserved 6,666 per class
datasets.split: Table 1; each Wikipedia page occurs in exactly one split; dev/test balanced 3,333 per class
datasets.source: June 2017 Wikipedia dump, intro sections of ~50,000 popular pages, processed with Stanford CoreNLP
datasets.preprocessing: Claims written by annotators with a dictionary of linked terms; six mutation types; NEI instances get simulated evidence (NEARESTP or RANDOMS) for RTE training

models.name: DrQA document retrieval
models.architecture: cosine similarity of binned unigram and bigram TF-IDF vectors

models.name: Sentence selection (DrQA bigram TF-IDF, or NLTK unigram TF-IDF)
models.architecture: TF-IDF similarity ranking of sentences to claim

models.name: Decomposable attention (DA)
models.architecture: Parikh et al. 2016 decomposable attention between claim and evidence

other.SNLI variant: AllenNLP pre-trained SNLI model used for comparison

models.name: MLP (Riedel et al. 2017)
models.architecture: single hidden layer MLP on term frequencies and TF-IDF cosine similarity

training.objective: 3-way classification of claim given concatenated evidence sentences
training.seeds: 5 random initialisations per model, best on dev reported (learning curve experiment)

other.NEI training evidence: NEARESTP (sentence from top-ranked retrieved page) or RANDOMS (random Wikipedia sentence)

inference.samples: single pipeline run on test; 5 initialisations in learning-curve study
inference.retrieval: k=5 documents, l=5 sentences, concatenated for RTE

eval.protocol: Oracle evaluations on dev per component; final pipeline on test; manual error analysis of 961 predictions; agreement by Fleiss kappa, super-annotators, author check of 227

limits: Evidence annotation is incomplete (annotator recall 72.36% vs super-annotators), so precision is penalised for valid extra evidence; authors advocate crowd-sourcing false positives later
Wikipedia intro sections only; authors say Wikipedia is not the only source and avoid TRUE/FALSE labels
NEI training evidence must be simulated; RANDOMS inflates oracle accuracy but hurts pipeline
Baseline is deliberately simple TF-IDF plus 2017 RTE models; dated by later neural retrievers and LLMs
Claims that were mis-specified: 3% of claims, 4.05% in error analysis, did not meet guidelines
No hyperparameters (optimizer, lr, epochs) reported for RTE models
